C0edc29b93b.judge_assessment: This lands. The cited Ohio statutes protect tenants or occupants whose possessory right has terminated; they do not by themselves create rights for a mere social guest or house companion. The brief tries to answer by characterizing Alice as an occupant at will or sufferance, but that characterization is the case’s key factual/legal hinge and is not separately nailed down by a lease, rent obligation, or other formal tenancy evidence on this record. If the court rejects that status theory, the Chapter 1923 / R.C. 5321.15 lockout theory collapses.

Cb114695143.judge_assessment: This is essentially the same fault line as a2, but focused on the statutory exclusion theory. The authority cited does support the proposition that a person entitled to immediate possession cannot self-help exclude a tenant and must proceed under Chapter 1923. The problem is the predicate status: the brief assumes Alice fits within R.C. 5321.15’s protection. If she is not within the protected class, the lock-change conduct is not a statutory violation on this record.

C846eb40a54.judge_assessment: The summary-judgment standard is correctly stated, and the cited authorities support the movant’s burden and the light-most-favorable rule. The attack has force only insofar as the brief largely asserts that there was a factual dispute without separately walking every claim element. But the brief does point to concrete record items: Alice’s affidavit and exhibits, Nixon’s lock-change admissions, Cazeau’s affidavit directing her removal, and the police statement. On this record, the court would likely treat this as a merits/materiality problem rather than a total failure of proof.

C69c6cce25c.judge_assessment: The conversion attack is not fatal on this record. Ohio conversion requires wrongful dominion or control inconsistent with the owner’s rights, and the brief does allege more than mere inconvenience: it says Alice identified specific items, that the appellees kept them, and that they were never returned while she was being locked out. The weakness is evidentiary specificity and direct proof of who controlled which item, not a complete absence of a conversion theory. A court could still view this as a triable issue, though the claim is less developed than the lockout theory.

C36fdfa7633.judge_assessment: This point has some support because hearsay is generally not admissible in summary-judgment proof. But it is not a strong attack here. The brief does not depend on the police statement alone; it also relies on the lockout notices, the repeated lock changes, Alice’s affidavit, and appellees’ own admissions. In addition, the statement is embedded in appellees’ pleading, so the evidentiary use is not as straightforwardly hearsay as the attack suggests. This would not likely drive the result.

C86daa34db6.judge_assessment: This does not move the needle on this record. The brief does more than say property was left behind: it says appellees kept the belongings and never returned them, after repeatedly changing the locks and preventing retrieval. That is the sort of evidence a court can treat as a factual dispute over dominion and control. The attack also overstates any need for a separate demand-and-refusal showing when the alleged control is tied to the exclusion itself.

Cadb3452ff4.judge_assessment: This attack misframes the statutory threshold. The brief does not rely on a formal landlord-tenant lease; it argues Alice was an occupant staying at Edwin's will or sufferance, and the cited Ohio forcible-entry-and-detainer provisions are broad enough to reach an occupier without color of title or another unlawful detention. On this record, the cohabitation facts are enough to create at least a factual issue on possession status, so the threshold challenge is not a clean summary-judgment win for appellees.

C23a951ba86.judge_assessment: This is not a strong appellate point here. The brief's response is that once conversion is shown, nominal damages are available and the amount of damages is for the factfinder. That is the ordinary way the issue is framed on summary judgment. The attack's reliance on 'no actual loss, no nominal damages' is not supported by the brief's cited authority as presented here, and it does not undercut the liability evidence the brief relies on.

C4417bac1a0.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The retrieved Ohio authority says that, absent a contrary agreement or law, prior owners of rental property are divested of all rights and obligations when title transfers. The brief's answer is not Ohio authority; it relies on Restatement nuisance principles and the proposition that Ohio courts may look to the Restatement. On this record, the court has a real basis to treat the former-owner-liability theory as an extension of Ohio law rather than an application of it.

Cb266174c05.judge_assessment: This is a serious duty problem. Ohio materials describe the traditional limits on landlord tort exposure and, separately, say prior-owner obligations end when title passes absent contrary law. The brief pleads a duty from knowledge and foreseeability, but its only real answer for a former owner is the same novel Restatement/nuisance extension discussed elsewhere. If the court refuses to recognize a continuing duty after transfer, this negligence claim fails on duty.

Cb94584e29d.judge_assessment: This attack has force, but it is not fatal on its own. The cited Cleveland ordinance and lead statutes do impose abatement/compliance duties, and the brief alleges Stark received the control order while it still owned the property and failed to abate before selling. The weak point is the jump from that pre-transfer noncompliance to a private damages claim against a former owner for later occupants. The brief partly answers by tying the violation to Stark's own conduct while it held title, but it still lacks Ohio authority squarely saying those enactments create continuing liability to later tenants or children after transfer.

C6ec450138a.judge_assessment: This is a good framing attack. The brief concedes there is no Ohio case expressly adopting Restatement § 840A, so the court would be extending Ohio law rather than applying settled precedent. Ohio materials also point the other way by treating ownership transfer as the cutoff for prior-owner obligations absent contrary law. The brief does answer in part with DiCenzo and other Restatement-friendly citations, but those are persuasive, not controlling.

C9e42ca592f.judge_assessment: This is weaker at the pleading stage. Ohio law does require a reasonable causal connection, but the brief expressly pleads causation and says material allegations and reasonable inferences must be taken as true on 12(C)/12(B)(6). The attack would matter more if the court were clearly in summary-judgment territory and the record still lacked evidence tying Stark's earlier conduct to the child's lead exposure. On this record, causation is a real issue, but not a clean dismissal ground by itself.

C27c450cc49.judge_assessment: This is the strongest defense point on the brief's nuisance/Restatement theory. The cited Ohio source says prior owners are divested of rights and obligations when title transfers absent a contrary law or agreement, which directly undercuts the brief's attempt to keep Stark liable after relinquishing the property. The brief does try to answer with Restatement §§ 840A and 373 plus out-of-state nuisance cases, but it does not supply an Ohio case adopting that post-transfer liability rule on this record. If the court accepts the Ohio transfer-cutoff premise, the nuisance theory falls at the threshold.

C6d7d9b3c3b.judge_assessment: The common-law negligence count stands or falls on duty, and the cited Ohio authority does not clearly recognize a general duty from a former owner to later occupants after transfer. The brief tries to bridge that gap with Restatement §§ 840A and 373 and policy arguments, but those are persuasive only if the court is willing to extend Ohio law. On this record, that is a real vulnerability because the claim seeks to impose liability after Stark no longer owned or possessed the premises. If the court rejects that extension, the negligence claim fails even if knowledge and injury are alleged.

C426cf0d9d3.judge_assessment: This point has some force, but it does not cleanly fit the brief's own timeline. The brief alleges Stark got the lead-hazard order while it still owned the property, received an extension, and then failed to abate before the sale/foreclosure. That means the negligence-per-se theory is not solely about a duty that survived transfer. The cited Ohio landlord-duty source does limit the statute to landlords, which helps the defense, but the brief's municipal-ordinance theory says 'No person shall fail to comply' with the commissioner’s order, and the brief says the noncompliance occurred before Stark relinquished title. So the attack is answerable, not fatal on this record.

Ce67cf676e6.judge_assessment: The causation attack is not the cleanest way to affirm on this record. The brief alleges the child was harmed by Stark's failure to remove or cover the lead hazards, and at the pleading stage those allegations are taken as true. If the court treats the motion as summary judgment, causation becomes a harder issue, but the brief also says it needed discovery to develop that evidence. So the defense argument has some merit as to proof, but it does not cleanly defeat the claim at the posture the brief is pressing. It is more of a merits problem than a dismissal-stage winner.

C92e7363c52.judge_assessment: This is only as strong as the underlying legal theory. If the court accepts the defense view that Stark owed no continuing post-transfer duty, then more discovery will not matter and a Rule 56(F) request cannot save the case. But the brief's 56(F) request is not frivolous on its face: it says Stark missed a deposition and that discovery was needed on duty, breach, and causation. So the defense point lands only if the court first accepts the transfer-cutoff argument; otherwise, denying discovery before deciding a converted summary-judgment motion would be harder to sustain.

C73fcb82f35.judge_assessment: This is the strongest procedural pushback. On this record, appellees cite App.R. 9(B), 13(B), and 16 and ask for dismissal/striking, but they do not cite a rule or case showing those defects automatically require dismissal rather than a lesser sanction or merits review. The brief does say appellant missed the transcript deadline, failed service, and filed a noncompliant brief, so the underlying complaints are answered factually; what is not fully answered is the authority for the requested end-stage sanction. If the court accepts the attack, appellees lose the shortcut to an outright dismissal and the appeal would move to the merits.

C1aca062b9b.judge_assessment: This attack has some traction, but it does not cleanly defeat the appellees’ rule as written. The appellees’ brief is narrower than the attack suggests: it says a condition-of-premises or repair defense may not be raised in this eviction unless the tenant used the escrow remedy under R.C. 5321.07, and it relies on Smith and Martins Ferry Jaycee Housing for that proposition. The cited source snippets invoked by the attack point to tenant remedies and habitability concepts generally, but they do not squarely establish that a tenant may assert repair/habitability issues as a defense to restitution without meeting the escrow requirement. So the attack is not frivolous, but on this record it does not clearly displace the appellees’ cited cases. If it landed, appellees would lose one of their main merits answers and the writ would be much more vulnerable.

Cab30413e11.judge_assessment: The strike request is broadly framed, but the core point is supported: appellate courts do not consider extra-record exhibits or factual assertions. The brief also identifies at least one concrete extra-record item—the November 20, 2006 inspection report—and says the garage-lease issue was not raised below. That means appellees have more than a bare blanket complaint. Still, the attack is fair to the extent the brief asks to strike everything wholesale without item-by-item record matching. The likely result, if the court is persuaded, is a narrower ruling: some attachments and claims get disregarded, but not necessarily every reference appellant made.

C66008bee72.judge_assessment: This lands. The cited authority does not actually support automatic dismissal or striking the appeal for the kinds of appellate-rule defects alleged here. Terry Brown v. Shauntel Dobbins is a Civ.R. 41(B)(1) want-of-prosecution case, not authority for a self-executing appellate sanction. On this record, the brief states the noncompliance and the missed court order, but it does not supply a real sanction analysis or authority tying those defects to dismissal rather than some lesser remedy.

Cc5939e0754.judge_assessment: This is a real vulnerability, though not as strong as a1. The brief piles up several procedural complaints, but it does not explain why dismissal and striking the brief are the proper sanctions as opposed to ignoring improper material or ordering compliance. That makes the requested relief look broader than what the record and cited authority presently justify. A court could still exercise discretion against a noncompliant appellant, but the brief has not shown why the harshest remedy is warranted here.

Cbd799e4e13.judge_assessment: This attack partially lands. Ohio law supports ignoring materials outside the record, but the request is broader than the showing on the page: the brief says the exhibits, photographs, and factual assertions are 'in large part' outside the record, which concedes not everything may be extra-record. A blanket strike of all attachments and all challenged assertions would overreach unless the court can identify each item as outside the record. The court is likely to prune specific items rather than accept a wholesale strike on this showing.

C1d50a54584.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. On this record, the brief does show protected activity, landlord knowledge, a nonrenewal notice, and later OCRC probable cause, but the causal link is still the weak point. The cited retaliation materials say timing matters and retaliation is often proved circumstantially, yet they do not make timing alone enough. A court could view the OCRC probable-cause finding as helpful but not dispositive, especially at summary judgment. If this lands, Masten loses the FHA retaliation theory that drives reversal.

Cdb171e49a2.judge_assessment: Ohio law generally does not require renewal of a fixed-term lease absent a contractual renewal clause, and the cited source supports that proposition. But the brief does not depend on a right to renewal as such; it tries to fit the nonrenewal into FHA retaliation/interference. So the attack lands only if the court accepts the premise that a lawful lease expiration cannot become unlawful absent an independent legal duty to renew. The brief partially answers by invoking § 3617 and persuasive nonrenewal-as-retaliation cases. If the attack wins, the federal retaliation theory fails at the threshold.

Cc66a3a25f0.judge_assessment: The preemption point is real only if federal law actually reaches the conduct at issue and state law blocks it. The cited preemption source supports the general Supremacy Clause framework, but the attack is weak to the extent it assumes the lack of an express federal renewal right ends the analysis. The brief’s answer is that § 3615 and § 3617 make a retaliatory nonrenewal unlawful, so a state rule that bars that defense conflicts with federal law. If the court agrees there is no actual conflict, the federal defense is gone; if it agrees with the brief, state holdover precedent yields.

C79f6387189.judge_assessment: This attack is narrower than it first sounds. It is true that the absence of R.C. 5321.03(A)(4)’s holdover language in Chapter 4112 does not by itself create a right to stay after lease expiration. But the brief is not really arguing that the absence alone creates a right; it argues the landlord-tenant holdover limitation should not be imported wholesale into fair-housing analysis. The attack therefore lands only against the doctrinal bridge, not against the whole theory. If accepted, the Ohio Fair Housing Act theory loses the argument that Indian Hills is inapplicable.

Ca4ae6bcbe2.judge_assessment: This is mostly a policy objection to overruling precedent, and it is not well anchored in the cited authority. The cited Ohio public-policy cases talk about contracts or witness intimidation, but they do not supply a doctrinal test for overruling Indian Hills. The brief already tries to repurpose those cases by analogizing retaliatory nonrenewal to witness intimidation. A court could reject the policy plea as too broad, but it is not a clean knockout because the brief is asking for reconsideration of precedent, not creating a lease-renewal right from scratch. If it lands, Masten loses the broadest route to overturn Indian Hills.

C2f82d360f8.judge_assessment: This is mostly a framing attack. The brief already says a nonrenewal can have the same practical effect as eviction and that motive matters when the nonrenewal follows protected activity; it also cites out-of-state and federal authority for that proposition. Source 23 does support that a landlord need not renew a fixed term lease absent agreement, but that does not answer whether a retaliatory nonrenewal can be actionable under fair-housing law. The attack therefore does not really defeat the theory; it just insists that expiration is not itself an eviction. If it lands, Masten loses the attempt to treat nonrenewal as the operative adverse act.

Cbbacd23a42.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The cited Ohio authority does support the landlord-tenant holdover framework, and the brief does not truly answer that framework so much as argue that federal law should trump it. On this record, if the court accepts source 2 and source 41's reading of Indian Hills/Siegler, Ms. Masten loses the central premise that a federal retaliation defense defeats the possession judgment once holdover status attached.

C858a16f84f.judge_assessment: The chronology in the brief itself helps the landlord. Ms. Masten's lease expired, notice was served, she did not vacate, and the eviction followed. That makes the case look like a standard post-expiration possession action, which is exactly the setting in which the Ohio holdover cases matter. The brief's answer is only to say the nonrenewal was retaliatory, so if retaliation proof fails, this chronology is fatal.

C7a30ab4723.judge_assessment: The supremacy argument is vulnerable because the brief never pins down a concrete conflict. The cited preemption authorities are broad, but source 4 does not itself show that Ohio law or Indian Hills actually requires discriminatory conduct or forbids federal rights. In this record, opposing counsel can plausibly say there is no direct conflict, only an argument that the state rule was applied incorrectly. If the court sees no actual conflict, the Supremacy Clause theory falls away.

C3a8009efc1.judge_assessment: This is a real summary-judgment attack on causation. Source 6 supports the need to prove retaliation, but the brief's proof is largely chronology, inference, and the OCRC probable-cause finding. That may be enough to get to a fact issue, but it is not the same as proving causation as a matter of law. Ms. Masten stands to lose if the court thinks the proof shows only protected activity followed by nonrenewal, not retaliatory causation.

C209d00ec4d.judge_assessment: The public-policy argument is the weakest theory because it asks the court to create a broad anti-retaliation exception on top of statutes and precedent that already occupy the field. The cited public-policy and witness-intimidation cases are far removed from a landlord's refusal to renew a lease, and the brief does not give the court a principled basis to overrule Indian Hills on policy alone. Ms. Masten stands to lose the fallback theory even if the statutory theories are found wanting.

Cf1bf4fee71.judge_assessment: This is a fair pushback, but it is not a knockout by itself. The brief's Chapter 4112 point depends on the claim that Indian Hills cannot be imported because the landlord-tenant holdover language is absent from the fair-housing statute. Opposing counsel can answer that silence does not create an affirmative holdover-defense right; it just means Chapter 4112 does not itself supply one. The brief loses some force here because the inferential step is thin.

Ce5a5b9c335.judge_assessment: This is directionally right but somewhat redundant with the causation attack. The cited authority supports that protected conduct alone does not make every later nonrenewal unlawful. The brief does answer with protected-activity facts and an asserted retaliatory sequence, but it does not bridge the gap with solid proof that the protected activity was the reason for the nonrenewal. Still, this is not as strong as the holdover or supremacy attacks because it mostly restates the causation problem.

Ca7d9b5f572.judge_assessment: This is the strongest preclusion attack. Ohio authority does not support the brief’s broad statement that Civ.R. 13(A) is simply irrelevant to all forcible-entry-and-detainer-related litigation; the retrieved sources say Civil Rules apply in FED cases unless clearly inapplicable, and R.C. 1923.081 expressly allows rent and damage claims to be tried with FED claims. The brief does answer in part by arguing Haney and by saying the present injury claim was not logically related to the earlier actions, and that some defendants were not parties to the FED case. But the hard problem remains the 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease action: if that suit included money claims, appellees have a real argument that the counterclaim rule mattered there. If the court accepts that framing, appellant loses the res judicata defense and the summary judgment becomes much harder to reverse.

Cefa1383b04.judge_assessment: The attack has real force because res ipsa loquitur in Ohio still requires exclusive control and a circumstance that ordinarily would not occur without negligence. The brief relies heavily on exclusive control of the storage room and the table, but the record also shows appellant was present in the room, several employees were present, and the table was being used elsewhere in the building. That makes the res ipsa theory less clean than the brief suggests. Still, on this record the appellees’ control evidence is not nonexistent: the room was locked, only staff had keys, and the evidence points to appellees’ control of the setting. So this attack does not automatically defeat appellant, but it exposes the brief’s weakest negligence theory and could matter if the court views the proof as too speculative.

C3fbc1d92b2.judge_assessment: This is a fair attack, but it is not a knockout. The brief does not identify the precise employee who allegedly caused the table to fall, and respondeat superior does require an employee tort committed within the scope of employment. On the other hand, the brief does tie the incident to employees who were managing access to the storage room and handling appellant’s belongings, which is at least some circumstantial evidence of scope. The problem is that the brief is thin on the actual tortious act and relies on inference. If the court views the incident as ordinary premises management by employees acting for the apartment complex, the theory survives; if it views the cause as unknown, the theory weakens considerably.

Ce873b033df.judge_assessment: The open-and-obvious point has some traction, but it does not cleanly carry appellees on this record. Ohio law turns on whether the danger itself was open and obvious, not merely whether the plaintiff was in the vicinity of the condition. The brief’s facts cut both ways: appellant saw the table and knew it was there, but the injury came when the table allegedly fell onto him. That is not the same as voluntarily walking into a plainly visible static hazard. The defense would argue that he knew of the table and chose to work around it on his knees, but the record as presented does not make the open-and-obvious doctrine a sure winner for appellees.

Ca2b6fb4f30.judge_assessment: This is largely cumulative of the main res judicata attack. It tries to broaden the transaction-or-occurrence analysis beyond the brief’s focus on common areas, but the brief already says the injury claim is not logically related to the rent litigation and not an off-shoot of the same controversy. The attack is not unsupported, but on this record it does not add much beyond a1 and is less likely to move the court independently. The court would probably treat it as part of the same preclusion dispute rather than a separate ground for affirmance.

Cedd94c7818.judge_assessment: This lands in part. The cited landlord-tenant materials do support a narrow rule that Civ.R. 13(A) is not applied to a pure forcible-entry-and-detainer case alleging only possession, but they do not by themselves establish a blanket immunity from compulsory-counterclaim treatment for a separate monetary back-rent/breach-of-lease action. The brief does answer with a fallback argument that the personal-injury claim was not logically related to the back-rent action, and that the parties differed in the FED case, but that answer is thin on the 2004 civil case. If the court accepts appellees' framing of the 2004 action as ordinary civil litigation, appellant risks losing the res judicata issue outright.

C7460ac1977.judge_assessment: This is a real pressure point. Hake requires exclusive control of the instrumentality causing the injury, and the brief mostly proves control of the storage room, not clearly control of the six-foot table at the moment it moved. The brief does point to Ball's testimony that the table was still used in the building's ballroom and to the admission that the room was under appellees' exclusive control, but that is not the same as proving exclusive control of the table as the relevant instrumentality. On this record, appellees have a meaningful argument that res ipsa cannot get past summary judgment.

Cba6237792b.judge_assessment: This also lands, though not perfectly. The governing element is whether the circumstances show the injury would not have occurred absent a lack of ordinary care. The brief relies on an unexplained table movement and then states, in conclusory fashion, that ordinary care would have prevented the injury. That is the weak spot appellees can press. The brief does have some supportive facts — the table was said to be where it should not have been, and employees controlled the room — but those facts do not by themselves establish the second Hake element as a matter of law. If the court agrees, the res ipsa theory falls.

C0d64fe8368.judge_assessment: This is a weaker attack on this record. The cited open-and-obvious rule is real, but appellees still have to show that the condition was so obvious that they owed no duty as a matter of law. A stationary six-foot folding table in a storage room is not obviously the same thing as a gaping hole or a wet floor, and the brief has a live response: appellant says the table struck him rather than that he knowingly chose to encounter a known hazard. That does not make the issue win for appellant, but it does make appellees' 'open and obvious' argument less than airtight here.

C38193a25de.judge_assessment: This is only partly persuasive. The brief does say landlords owe invitees ordinary care and must warn of latent defects, but appellees can reasonably respond that the brief never identifies a latent defect or concealed hazard at all; it describes a visible table in a room the tenant was directed into. Still, the negligence theory is not limited to latent defects if the claim is framed as active negligence or negligent control of the room during the cleanup. So the attack does not fully defeat the negligence claim, but it does expose a gap in the brief's duty/breach discussion.

C8d46162188.judge_assessment: This has real force. Ohio materials do recognize oral rental agreements and an employee-tenant concept, so the brief cannot rely on 'no written lease' and 'no rent' as a complete legal answer by themselves. The brief does say there was no oral or written rental agreement, no rent, a separate residence, and only an employment accommodation, which helps it, but it never separately confronts the employee-tenant theory. On this record, the court could see that as an underdeveloped gap if appellant produced any evidence that the housing was part of the employment contract.

C972f3537ba.judge_assessment: This is the most outcome-driving attack. Summary judgment turns on whether the caregiver arrangement was legally a tenancy or merely permissive employment-based occupancy. The brief's facts favor appellees, but they do not make the legal issue one-sided as a matter of law if Ohio recognizes employee tenancy or oral housing arrangements tied to employment. If appellant had evidence supporting that theory, the no-tenancy conclusion is not compelled on summary judgment.

C405b06fe56.judge_assessment: The analogy attack has some bite because the brief's main authorities are rent-free occupancy cases, not an employee-housing case. But the brief does answer in part by insisting that the common feature in those cases is the absence of a rental agreement and rent, and by distinguishing commercial premises cases. The court is unlikely to reject the brief just because the cases are not identical; the real question is whether the factual differences matter enough to defeat the no-tenancy rule.

C5b80071967.judge_assessment: This is mostly answered already. The brief does not claim that the word 'may' in R.C. 1923.02(A) authorizes self-help; it uses the phrase to argue that Chapter 1923 lists permissible proceedings and that R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED exclusive only in the landlord-tenant situation. The opponent's point that the statute is not a permission slip for bypassing all statutory process is fair as a general reading, but it does not really defeat the brief's narrower exclusivity argument.

C7d5b7e6b89.judge_assessment: This attack does not land well on this record. It is true that R.C. 1923.02(A) includes occupiers as a class subject to FED, but the brief is not denying that FED can be used against occupiers. Its point is that FED is not the exclusive remedy absent a residential tenancy under Chapter 5321. So the occupier language does not undercut the brief's exclusivity theory the way the attack suggests.

C41dc315bc5.judge_assessment: This is largely rhetorical. The brief expressly says Reynolds is factually and procedurally different and that Metcalf is an out-of-state federal case involving California unlawful-detainer procedures and Section 1983 claims. Using Metcalf as a factual illustration while rejecting it as controlling authority is not a serious flaw on this record.

C4ed86604e5.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Ohio authority in the supplied sources does support that a rental agreement may be oral or implied, and the legal materials also recognize an employee tenant. That undercuts appellees' categorical no-lease/no-rent framing. The brief tries to answer with Ogle and the facts that no rent was paid and appellant kept a separate residence, but it does not really confront the employee-tenant theory or explain why employment-based occupancy cannot satisfy tenancy on this record. If appellant can tie the occupancy to a contract of employment that functioned as a rental arrangement, summary judgment is vulnerable.

Cae094519da.judge_assessment: This attack goes to the core summary-judgment burden. Appellees say the absence of a written lease and rent ends the matter, but the Ohio materials supplied here make clear that tenancy can arise from an oral or implied rental agreement and that employee tenancy is a recognized concept. The brief's response is largely a restatement of its no-rent/no-lease facts; it does not eliminate the possibility that appellant occupied the room under an employment-based tenancy. If a court sees that as a genuine issue, appellees lose the basis for affirmance on Counts II, V, VI, and VII.

C32f6899799.judge_assessment: This is a viable legal-framing challenge. The brief's FED argument is only as strong as its premise that no tenancy existed. But the supplied Ohio materials say rental agreements can be oral and that employment-based occupancy can create employee tenancy. So the 'formal lease only' framing is too narrow. The brief does answer by citing R.C. 5321.15(A) and the line of cases holding FED is exclusive only in the residential-tenant setting, but that answer does not resolve whether appellant fits within that setting. If the court accepts the broader tenant concept, appellees lose the argument that they could bypass FED as a matter of law.

Ca9460b0565.judge_assessment: This is a fair narrowing attack. The cited cases in the brief are rent-free/no-lease occupant cases; they do not by themselves establish a universal rule that every rent-free occupant is a non-tenant. The supplied Ohio materials also recognize employee tenancy and oral or implied rental agreements. The brief answers partly by stressing that appellant was a former employee and by analogizing to Ogle, Stone, and Amick, but that answer is incomplete if the employee-tenant theory has evidentiary support. The advocate risks losing the ability to treat those cases as controlling precedent for this fact pattern.

Cb2973c3657.judge_assessment: This is the core vulnerability in the possession theory. Ohio authority cited in the brief does support the general proposition that present title can control possession when title is the issue, but the brief still has to prove that the probate orders and the February 1, 2023 deed actually vested present title in the Estate as a matter of law. On this record, that step is asserted more than demonstrated. If the court is not satisfied that title was effectively transferred, the Estate loses the main legal basis for summary judgment on possession and the requested writ of restitution.

C91798f29b2.judge_assessment: This attack lands, but only if the defendants can show the notice did not use one of R.C. 1923.04(A)'s permitted delivery methods. The cited authority supports strict compliance with the three-day notice requirement and the statutory warning language. The brief answers part of the point by giving the date, the premises location, and the warning language, but it is thinner on the precise service method. If the exhibit shows a noncompliant method, the Estate loses the statutory prerequisite for the FED case; if it shows service by leaving the notice at the premises or another listed method, the attack fails.

C9a7725597e.judge_assessment: This is the weakest legal link in the possession argument, and it is fair game. Sed v. Mundy supports a superior right to possession where the estate was empowered to sell the property, but the brief stretches that rationale to a broader management order. The cited authority does not clearly say that inventorying, collecting rents, paying taxes, and making repairs alone creates a present possessory right against occupants. The brief partly answers by saying the probate court empowered the Estate to manage and sell the Premises, but the management-to-possession step is still inferential. If the court rejects that inference, the Estate loses this alternative basis for possession even if title is uncertain.

C6b1a6f8492.judge_assessment: This is more of a framing objection than a real legal defect. The cited Civ.R. 56 authorities do not say a motion automatically wins just because it is supported by affidavits and exhibits, and the brief does not actually rely on a bare recitation; it goes on to identify title, deed, and notice facts. The attack would only matter if those facts were not actually admissible or did not eliminate a genuine issue. As written, it is mostly answered by the brief's later factual sections. The Estate would only lose if the court concluded the record is too thin to support summary judgment, not because the brief used the wrong standard.

C29c93a22d7.judge_assessment: This is a cumulative restatement of the earlier attacks, not a separate defect. The brief's requested relief does depend on title and notice, but the motion already says those elements are satisfied and supports them with the deed, probate orders, and notice facts. If the court accepts those showings, the conclusion follows. If it rejects them, this attack adds nothing beyond a2, a3, and a4. The Estate stands to lose only the same possession judgment and writ already at issue in those specific challenges.

C5be43f3a3b.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The cited authority does support the general proposition that present title controls present possession and that title disputes may have to be resolved before eviction, and the brief itself tries to answer with Wayne, Gordon, and Sed. But on this record the weak point is exactly what the attack says: the court is being asked to treat execution/filing/safekeeping of the deed as effective delivery of title without a clear factual showing that delivery was legally operative. If the court is not convinced title passed, the Estate loses the core predicate for possession.

C3d36571501.judge_assessment: This is a real Civ.R. 56 vulnerability, not a made-up one. The cited materials support the proposition that summary-judgment evidence must be competent and that evidentiary rules still matter in FED cases. The brief says the motion incorporates affidavits and exhibits by reference, but it does not itself demonstrate that the counsel affidavit is based on personal knowledge or that all incorporated materials are properly authenticated. If those affidavits are stricken or discounted, a lot of the factual foundation for title, possession, and notice disappears.

C37fdff2c06.judge_assessment: The statute cited does require that defendants be occupiers without color of title, and Dresher puts the burden on the movant to show the absence of a genuine issue. The brief mostly answers this by saying defendants are not title holders and by relying on the probate rulings and deed transfer, but it does not separately develop why defendants lack color of title. If the title showing fails or is viewed as incomplete, this element is exposed.

C05dd981e98.judge_assessment: The notice issue is fact-sensitive and can defeat the eviction if compliance is not proved. The statute supports the service-method requirement, and the brief says service was by certified mail, return receipt requested, on June 28, 2023, with the proper warning language. The attack is narrower: the excerpt shown here does not itself include the receipt or mailing proof. That makes this an evidentiary sufficiency attack, not a statutory misread. If the exhibits really show the mailing and proper content, the attack fails; if they do not, it matters a lot.

C1a1d7058fc.judge_assessment: This is mostly derivative of the title and notice attacks. The cited authority does support that a writ of restitution follows only after the right to possession is established, so if the predicate issues fail, the remedy fails too. But the brief already asks for the writ only after obtaining summary judgment on possession, so this does not add an independent defect. It only matters if the court rejects the underlying possession showing.

C182de6eb12.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Ohio authority does require a same-transaction/logical-relation showing before Civ.R. 13(A) makes a claim compulsory, and the cited cases are the right category of authority. The brief partly answers by saying Friese's injury claim arose from the tenancy, by noting his invitee status came from the landlord-tenant relationship, and by relying on Sherman/Haney/Adams. But the record as presented still does not spell out the prior municipal complaint closely enough to make the transaction-or-occurrence link airtight. If the court is not willing to infer that a rent/property-damage eviction case and a later premises-injury tort claim are the same transaction, Baker loses the res judicata ground entirely.

Cebdfef6327.judge_assessment: The attack has real force to the extent Baker is trying to state a blanket rule that landlords have no statutory duty to install a handrail. The cited materials do not support a universal no-duty rule; R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and the landlord-tenant materials recognize code-compliance duties, and the retrieved authority specifically flags handrails as a potential code issue in some cases. But the brief already narrows its point: it says Friese did not plead a landlord-code theory and that, under St. Germain and Taylor, the habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) does not reach a missing handrail. So this only lands if the complaint or local code actually supplies a handrail-duty theory.

C465d27be04.judge_assessment: This is a narrower version of the same problem. Armstrong does support the open-and-obvious doctrine for ordinary premises-liability claims, but the retrieved landlord-tenant authority correctly notes that open-and-obvious principles do not defeat statutory negligence-per-se claims under R.C. 5321.04. Baker's brief answers by insisting Friese pleaded only invitee premises liability and by saying his awareness of the stairs and missing railing makes the hazard open and obvious. On this record, the attack does not defeat the motion unless Friese can tie the claim to a specific statutory or code-based handrail duty.

C0dc69a2210.judge_assessment: This is the most consequential attack. The cited landlord-tenant materials do support the proposition that not every tenant claim is compulsory, and one source expressly says Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply where the eviction complaint seeks only possession. The brief, however, does more than rely on a bare possession case: it says Baker’s earlier municipal action also sought monetary damages and ended in a merits judgment, and it cites the Sherman/Haney line for the proposition that a tenant injury claim tied to the rental relationship can be a compulsory counterclaim. So the attack does not defeat the theory outright, but it does expose the weakest factual/legal step: whether Friese’s fall claim truly arose out of the same transaction or occurrence as Baker’s eviction-and-damages action. If the court is not persuaded on that connection, Baker loses the res judicata/counterclaim defense.

C122ec7fcc7.judge_assessment: Authority supports the general open-and-obvious rule, but the attack lands on the brief’s weakest move: equating familiarity with the stairs to knowledge of the alleged missing-handrail hazard. The brief does have a response—Friese allegedly told Baker the staircase needed a railing, used the steps multiple times daily, and said he knew their condition. But it does not squarely confront the point that Friese also testified he noticed nothing unusual or particularly dangerous and did not know why he fell. On this record, that makes the duty question close enough that a court could view the handrail issue as disputed rather than open-and-obvious as a matter of law. Baker stands to lose summary judgment on the premises-liability claim.

Cf5d15710d7.judge_assessment: This is a summary-judgment wrapper attack rather than an independent defect. It is legally correct as a general proposition that Baker must show no genuine issue of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, but the motion already recites Civ.R. 56 and points to deposition testimony plus certified municipal-court records. The attack adds little unless the court first rejects the substantive defenses. On this record, it is mostly derivative: if the open-and-obvious and preclusion arguments survive, this challenge goes nowhere; if they fail, summary judgment fails for the same reason. Baker does not lose anything separate from the underlying merits defenses.
